title: The self-learning trap: when courses become expensive entertainment
description: Judge whether another course closes a real skill gap, when to build proof instead, and how to avoid treating course completion as progress.
body:
Judge whether another course closes a real skill gap, when to build proof instead, and how to avoid treating course completion as progress.

The tab with forty courses

On a Sunday night, a professional opens a learning platform and discovers a shelf of unfinished courses. Buying the next one feels like movement because it creates a clean beginning. The harder question is what work the previous course changed. Learning becomes expensive entertainment when consumption provides relief from the risk of being judged on an actual result. The difference between exposure and capability

When breadth is the right move

The hidden cost is attention

The fee is only one cost. Evening study competes with sleep, family, recovery, and the work that produces the evidence an employer can evaluate. Add the cost of tools, exams, commuting, and time away from an actual portfolio. A cheap course can be expensive if it displaces the project that mattered. The peer who ships less but learns more

Two colleagues take the same course. One completes every quiz. The other stops halfway to test a narrow idea, records a failure, and asks a domain expert to critique it. What durable learning feels like

The decision memo

Keep the course only if its cost, time, and opportunity cost fit the life around it and if a real assignment is waiting. Otherwise pause without shame. Not completing a course is not failure when the learner has discovered that the desired career needs evidence, context, and feedback rather than another polished lesson.
